glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: The LORD answers Moses’ distress by renewing His promise in His own name: He will bring Israel out, redeem them, take them as His people, and bring them into the land, so that they will know that He is the LORD.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Exodus 6 answers Moses’ prayer at the end of chapter 5, after Pharaoh has made Israel’s labor heavier. A family record of Levi then identifies Moses and Aaron.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Exodus 6:1–8 — The LORD Renews His Promise of Redemption

  • Exodus 6:9–13 — The People Cannot Listen, and Moses Is Sent Again

  • Exodus 6:14–27 — The Family Record of Moses and Aaron

  • Exodus 6:28–30 — The Narrative Returns to Moses’ Objection

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “I will take you as My people, and I will be your God. Then you shall know that I am the LORD your God who brings you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.” (Exodus 6:7)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Moses had asked why God sent him, and God’s answer begins with His name: “I am the LORD” (6:2). He appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty, but they had not experienced the full meaning of His name LORD. Now He will show what that name means by what He does. The promises tumble out: He will bring them out, rescue them, and “redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great judgments” (6:6). Then comes the heart of it all: “I will take you as My people, and I will be your God” (6:7). The rescue is for the sake of belonging. God frames the whole promise with His name, beginning and ending with “I am the LORD.”

The people cannot take it in. They do not listen “because of anguish of spirit and cruel bondage” (6:9), and Scripture treats their weariness with compassion. Moses, discouraged, protests again that he has “uncircumcised lips” (6:12). God does not withdraw His word. A family record interrupts the scene to locate Moses and Aaron within Levi’s line, then states plainly, “These are the same Moses and Aaron” (6:27). God’s promise does not depend on how strong His people or His servants feel.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Exodus 6:1–8 — The LORD Renews His Promise of Redemption

The LORD tells Moses that he will now see what God will do to Pharaoh, and He renews His promise under His name LORD. He pledges to bring Israel out of bondage, redeem them with great judgments, take them as His own people, and bring them into the land sworn to their fathers.

Exodus 6:9–13 — The People Cannot Listen, and Moses Is Sent Again

Israel does not listen to Moses because their spirit is crushed and their slavery is cruel. When the LORD sends Moses to Pharaoh again, Moses protests that his lips are unfit, and the LORD gives both Moses and Aaron His command to bring Israel out.

Exodus 6:14–27 — The Family Record of Moses and Aaron

A record of the heads of Israel’s families moves from Reuben and Simeon to Levi and traces the line through Kohath and Amram to Aaron and Moses and Aaron’s sons. It closes by identifying these as the very men the LORD sent to bring Israel out and to speak to Pharaoh.

Exodus 6:28–30 — The Narrative Returns to Moses’ Objection

The account returns to the day the LORD commanded Moses to speak all His words to Pharaoh. Moses again protests that his lips are unfit and asks how Pharaoh will listen, setting up God’s answer in chapter 7.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Exodus 6 shows that God’s answer to discouragement is a fresh word about who He is and what He will do. Moses’ circumstances had not changed, but God restated His purpose in the strongest terms. The goal of redemption is relationship: God takes a people as His own and gives Himself to them as their God, the same promise that reaches its fullness in the new covenant (Revelation 21:3).

The chapter is also gentle with people too crushed to listen. Israel’s failure to listen is explained, not condemned, by their anguish and their bondage. God keeps working on behalf of people who cannot yet hear His promise. The genealogy reminds readers that God works through real families and real history.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
The name of the LORD. God opens and closes His promise with “I am the LORD” and will make His name known by redeeming Israel (6:2–8).

Redemption and belonging. God promises to bring out, rescue, redeem, take as His people, and bring into the land (6:6–8).

God remembers His covenant. The LORD has heard Israel’s groaning and remembered His promise to the fathers (6:4–5).

Crushed spirits and renewed commission. The people cannot listen, and Moses feels unfit, yet God sends him again (6:9–13, 28–30).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
God Almighty (6:3). The name under which God appeared to the patriarchs (compare Genesis 17:1). The fathers knew the name LORD, but they had not yet experienced its full meaning as God now displays it in redemption.

Redeem (6:6). To free someone from bondage by paying a price or exercising power. Here God redeems Israel “with an outstretched arm and with great judgments.”

Uncircumcised lips (6:12, 30). A Hebrew way of describing lips that feel unqualified or unfit to speak for God (compare Isaiah 6:5).

The genealogy (6:14–27). A family record that narrows from Reuben and Simeon to Levi to place Moses and Aaron within Israel. It names Korah and Aaron’s sons, who appear later in the story.

focus: Exodus 6 gives the LORD’s answer to Moses’ distress: He renews His promise to bring Israel out, redeem them, take them as His people, and bring them into the land, so that they will know that He is the LORD. When the crushed people cannot listen and Moses doubts that Pharaoh will hear him, a genealogy identifies Moses and Aaron as the men God has sent, and the chapter returns to Moses’ objection.

sections.title: The LORD Renews His Promise of Redemption
sections.summary: The LORD tells Moses, “Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh” (Exodus 6:1), and declares that He who appeared to the fathers as God Almighty will now make His name LORD known by bringing Israel out of bondage. He promises, “I will take you as My people, and I will be your God” (Exodus 6:7), and swears to bring them into the land He promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

sections.title: The People Cannot Listen, and Moses Is Sent Again
sections.summary: Israel does not heed Moses “because of anguish of spirit and cruel bondage” (Exodus 6:9). When the LORD sends him to Pharaoh, Moses protests that he is “of uncircumcised lips” (Exodus 6:12), and the LORD gives Moses and Aaron a command to bring the children of Israel out of Egypt.

sections.title: The Family Record of Moses and Aaron
sections.summary: A list of the heads of fathers’ houses moves from Reuben and Simeon to Levi and traces the line of Kohath and Amram to Aaron and Moses and to Aaron’s descendants. It ends by declaring, “These are the same Moses and Aaron” (Exodus 6:27), the men the LORD commanded to bring Israel out and who spoke to Pharaoh.

sections.title: The Narrative Returns to Moses’ Objection
sections.summary: The account resumes on the day the LORD spoke to Moses in Egypt and commanded him to speak all His words to Pharaoh. Moses again protests that he is of uncircumcised lips and asks, “how shall Pharaoh heed me?” (Exodus 6:30).

1.brief: The LORD answers Moses, “Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh,” and declares that with a strong hand Pharaoh will let Israel go and even drive them out. God answers Moses’ complaint with a promise of His own powerful action.
1.explain:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh.”

The LORD does not rebuke Moses for his honest complaint (5:22–23). He answers with a promise. “Now” marks a turning point. Moses has seen what Pharaoh can do. Now he will see what God will do.

“For with a strong hand he will let them go, and with a strong hand he will drive them out of his land.”

Pharaoh had refused to let Israel go. God says that under the pressure of His “strong hand,” Pharaoh will not only release them but “drive them out.” The king who would not let them leave will one day push them out. This happened on the night of the Passover (12:31–33). God answers Moses’ complaint with a promise of His own powerful action.
1.notes: The phrase “strong hand” appears twice in this verse. It is unclear in Hebrew whether the first refers to God’s hand on Pharaoh or Pharaoh’s hand on Israel. Either way, God’s power stands behind the release.

2.brief: God speaks to Moses and says, “I am the LORD.” His renewed promise begins with His own name, the foundation for everything He is about to say.
2.explain:
“And God spoke to Moses and said to him: ‘I am the LORD.”

God begins His renewed promise with His name: “I am the LORD.” Everything He is about to promise rests on who He is. The phrase will frame this whole speech, appearing again in 6:6 and 6:8. Moses had questioned why God had not acted. God answers by reminding him whom he is dealing with.
2.notes: “I am the LORD” is a formula of self-identification found often in the books of Moses, especially in Leviticus (for example, Leviticus 18:2–5). It grounds God’s commands and promises in His own name.

3.brief: God says He appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty, “but by My name LORD I was not known to them.” The patriarchs knew the name, but they had not yet experienced its full meaning, which God now displays by redeeming Israel.
3.explain:
“I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, as God Almighty,”

God reminds Moses of His dealings with the fathers. He appeared to them “as God Almighty.” This name, El Shaddai in Hebrew, appears in God’s promises to Abraham and Jacob (Genesis 17:1; 35:11). It speaks of God’s power to fulfill what He promises.

“but by My name LORD I was not known to them.”

This does not mean the patriarchs never heard the name LORD. The name appears in their stories (Genesis 15:7; 28:13). The patriarchs knew the name, but they had not yet experienced its full meaning. They saw some of God’s promises kept, such as the birth of Isaac. But the promises named in 6:4–8, the land and the redemption of their descendants, they did not live to see fulfilled. Now God will display the meaning of His name by redeeming Israel and keeping His word. Israel will know Him as the LORD by what He does for them (6:7).
3.notes:
Some interpreters read the clause as a question expecting a yes, asking whether God was not known to the fathers by His name. The NKJV reading, understood as the full experience of the name, fits the following promises.

The Hebrew name El Shaddai is traditionally translated “God Almighty.” Its exact derivation is debated.

4.brief: God says He established His covenant with the patriarchs to give them the land of Canaan, where they lived as strangers. His promise of the land stands behind everything He is about to do.
4.explain:
“I have also established My covenant with them,”

God reminds Moses that He made a binding promise with the patriarchs. A “covenant” is a solemn commitment. God bound Himself to them by His own word.

“to give them the land of Canaan, the land of their pilgrimage, in which they were strangers.”

The covenant included “the land of Canaan.” The patriarchs lived there as “strangers,” foreigners who did not own the land. It was “the land of their pilgrimage,” the land where they wandered. They died without possessing it. God’s promise of the land stands behind everything He is about to do.
4.notes: The phrase “the land of their pilgrimage” reads literally the land of their sojournings. Abraham bought only a burial place there (Genesis 23).

5.brief: God says He has heard the groaning of Israel in bondage and has remembered His covenant. His hearing and remembering repeat Exodus 2:24 and show that He is about to act.
5.explain:
“And I have also heard the groaning of the children of Israel whom the Egyptians keep in bondage,”

God has heard the “groaning” of His people. The word recalls 2:24, where God heard their groaning. Their suffering has reached God’s ears.

“and I have remembered My covenant.”

God has “remembered” His covenant. As in 2:24, to remember means that God now turns to act on His promise. His hearing and remembering show that He is about to act.

6.brief: God tells Moses to say, “I am the LORD,” and promises, “I will bring you out,” rescue them from bondage, and redeem them with an outstretched arm and great judgments. The promises describe a complete deliverance by God’s own power.
6.explain:
“Therefore say to the children of Israel: ‘I am the LORD;”

God gives Moses a message for Israel. It begins again with God’s name. Before God tells them what He will do, He tells them who He is.

“I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians,”

The first promise: God will bring them “out from under the burdens,” the crushing forced labor (1:11; 5:4).

“I will rescue you from their bondage,”

The second promise: God will “rescue” them from slavery. He will snatch them out of Egypt’s grip.

“and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great judgments.”

The third promise: God will “redeem” them. To redeem means to set free by paying a price or by acting as a family protector. In Israel, a kinsman redeemer bought back a relative who had fallen into slavery (Leviticus 25:47–49). God acts as Israel’s Redeemer, the family member who comes to free His people.

He will do it “with an outstretched arm,” a picture of power in action, and “with great judgments” on Egypt. The promises describe a complete deliverance by God’s own power.
6.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “redeem” is the word used for the kinsman redeemer, the family member who protects and recovers what belongs to his relatives (for example, Ruth 3:9–13; 4:4–6). This is its first use in Exodus. Moses’ song later celebrates the people “whom You have redeemed” (15:13).

7.brief: God promises, “I will take you as My people, and I will be your God,” so that they will know that He is the LORD who brought them out. The goal of deliverance is a relationship in which Israel belongs to God and knows Him.
7.explain:
“I will take you as My people, and I will be your God.”

God’s purpose goes beyond rescue. God does not only free Israel from Egypt. He takes them for Himself. This promise is the heart of God’s relationship with His people throughout Scripture. It appears again at the end of the Bible: “they shall be His people. God Himself will be with them and be their God” (Revelation 21:3).

“Then you shall know that I am the LORD your God who brings you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.”

Through the deliverance Israel “shall know” God. They will know Him by experience as the God who rescued them. The goal of deliverance is a relationship in which Israel belongs to God and knows Him.
7.notes: The language of 6:7 resembles marriage and adoption formulas, in which one party takes another as his own.

8.brief: God promises to bring them into the land He swore to give Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and to give it to them as a heritage, ending again, “I am the LORD.” The promises that began with His name end with His name.
8.explain:
“And I will bring you into the land which I swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob;”

God will bring them “into the land.” He “swore” to give it to the fathers. The word pictures raising the hand in a solemn oath. God had promised, and He would keep His word.

“and I will give it to you as a heritage: I am the LORD.”

The land will be Israel’s “heritage,” a possession passed down to their children. The speech ends as it began: “I am the LORD.” The promises that began with His name end with His name.
8.notes: The Hebrew phrase behind “which I swore” reads literally which I lifted My hand, a gesture used in taking an oath.

9.brief: Moses speaks these words to Israel, “but they did not heed Moses, because of anguish of spirit and cruel bondage.” The narrator explains their failure to listen by their crushed spirit and harsh slavery.
9.explain:
“So Moses spoke thus to the children of Israel;”

Moses delivered God’s message faithfully.

“but they did not heed Moses, because of anguish of spirit and cruel bondage.”

The people “did not heed Moses.” Earlier they had believed and worshiped (4:31). Now they could not listen. The narrator explains why: “anguish of spirit,” literally shortness of spirit, and “cruel bondage.” Their spirits were crushed, and their slavery was harsh. The narrator explains their failure to listen with compassion. They were not stubborn like Pharaoh. They were broken.
9.notes: The Hebrew phrase translated “anguish of spirit” reads literally shortness of breath or of spirit. It describes discouragement and exhaustion.

10.brief: The LORD speaks to Moses again. God continues to direct Moses even after the people fail to listen.
10.explain:
“And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,”

God speaks again. Even when the people would not listen, God continued to direct Moses. God’s purpose did not depend on the people’s mood.

11.brief: The LORD tells Moses to go and tell Pharaoh to let the children of Israel go out of his land. The commission is renewed in the middle of the people’s discouragement.
11.explain:
“Go in, tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the children of Israel go out of his land.”

God renews the commission. Moses must go back to “Pharaoh king of Egypt” with the same demand. Nothing has changed in God’s plan. The commission is renewed in the middle of the people’s discouragement.

12.brief: Moses protests that if Israel has not heeded him, Pharaoh will not either, “for I am of uncircumcised lips.” He describes himself as unfit to speak, returning to his earlier objection about his speech.
12.explain:
“And Moses spoke before the LORD, saying, ‘The children of Israel have not heeded me.”

Moses objects. If his own people will not listen, why would Pharaoh?

“How then shall Pharaoh heed me, for I am of uncircumcised lips?”

Moses calls himself “of uncircumcised lips.” In Scripture, “uncircumcised” can describe something unfit or closed. Uncircumcised ears do not hear (Jeremiah 6:10). Moses describes his lips as unfit to speak. He returns to his earlier objection about his speech (4:10).
12.notes: The phrase “uncircumcised lips” appears only here and in 6:30. A similar image describes uncircumcised hearts (Leviticus 26:41) and ears (Jeremiah 6:10).

13.brief: The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them a command concerning Israel and Pharaoh, to bring Israel out of Egypt. God answers Moses’ protest by restating the charge to both brothers.
13.explain:
“Then the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, and gave them a command for the children of Israel and for Pharaoh king of Egypt,”

God answers by speaking to “Moses and Aaron” together. He gives them “a command.” He does not argue with Moses’ objection. He simply restates the charge.

“to bring the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt.”

The purpose stays the same. God answers Moses’ protest by restating the charge to both brothers.

14.brief: A record of the heads of Israel’s fathers’ houses begins with the sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn. The genealogy pauses the narrative to place Moses and Aaron within the families of Israel.
14.explain:
“These are the heads of their fathers’ houses:”

The narrative pauses for a genealogy. “The heads of their fathers’ houses” are the leaders of the extended families. The genealogy places Moses and Aaron within the families of Israel.

“The sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel, were Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. These are the families of Reuben.”

The list begins with Reuben, “the firstborn of Israel.” His four sons are named, matching Genesis 46:9.
14.notes: The genealogy follows the order of Jacob’s sons but stops after Levi. Its purpose is to identify Moses and Aaron, not to give a full record of all the tribes (6:26–27).

15.brief: The sons of Simeon are listed next, including Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. The record moves through Jacob’s sons in order toward Levi.
15.explain:
“And the sons of Simeon were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanite woman.”

Simeon’s six sons are named. One is singled out as “the son of a Canaanite woman,” matching Genesis 46:10.

“These are the families of Simeon.”

The record moves through Jacob’s sons in order toward Levi.

16.brief: The names of the sons of Levi are given, Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, along with Levi’s age of 137 years. The record now narrows to the tribe of Moses and Aaron.
16.explain:
“These are the names of the sons of Levi according to their generations: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.”

Now the genealogy reaches Levi, the tribe of Moses and Aaron. Levi had three sons. Their descendants would later serve in the tabernacle in distinct roles (Numbers 3–4).

“And the years of the life of Levi were one hundred and thirty-seven.”

Levi’s age is given. The record now narrows to the tribe of Moses and Aaron.
16.notes: Ages are given only for Levi, Kohath, and Amram, the direct line to Moses and Aaron.

17.brief: The sons of Gershon, Libni and Shimi, are listed by their families. The first branch of Levi’s family is recorded before the genealogy follows Kohath.
17.explain:
“The sons of Gershon were Libni and Shimi according to their families.”

Gershon’s two sons are listed. The first branch of Levi’s family is recorded before the genealogy follows Kohath.

18.brief: The sons of Kohath are Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, and Kohath lived 133 years. Amram, the father of Moses and Aaron, is now named.
18.explain:
“And the sons of Kohath were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel.”

Kohath’s four sons are named. The first is Amram, the father of Moses and Aaron.

“And the years of the life of Kohath were one hundred and thirty-three.”

Kohath’s age is recorded.
18.notes: The Kohathites would later carry the most holy furnishings of the tabernacle (Numbers 4:4–15).

19.brief: The sons of Merari, Mahli and Mushi, complete the families of Levi. The record has now named all three branches of the tribe.
19.explain:
“The sons of Merari were Mahli and Mushi.”

Merari’s two sons complete the list of Levi’s grandsons.

“These are the families of Levi according to their generations.”

The record has now named all three branches of the tribe.

20.brief: Amram marries Jochebed, his father’s sister, and she bears Aaron and Moses, and Amram lives 137 years. The genealogy reaches the two men God has sent and names their mother.
20.explain:
“Now Amram took for himself Jochebed, his father’s sister, as wife;”

Amram married “Jochebed, his father’s sister.” She was his aunt. Such a marriage was later forbidden in the law (Leviticus 18:12). The record states it plainly without comment.

“and she bore him Aaron and Moses.”

The genealogy reaches the two men God has sent. Aaron is named first because he was the older brother (7:7).

“And the years of the life of Amram were one hundred and thirty-seven.”

Amram’s age is given. The genealogy names the parents of Israel’s deliverers.
20.notes:
Some Greek and Latin manuscripts call Jochebed Amram’s cousin rather than his aunt. The Hebrew text reads “his father’s sister.”

Genealogies in Scripture sometimes skip generations. The four generations from Levi to Moses (Levi, Kohath, Amram, Moses) may name only the key links in a longer line.

21.brief: The sons of Izhar are Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri. Korah is named here among Moses’ close relatives.
21.explain:
“The sons of Izhar were Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.”

Izhar’s sons are named. Korah will later lead a rebellion against Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16). He is named here among Moses’ close relatives.

22.brief: The sons of Uzziel are Mishael, Elzaphan, and Zithri. The record continues to name the households of the Kohathites.
22.explain:
“And the sons of Uzziel were Mishael, Elzaphan, and Zithri.”

Uzziel’s sons are named. Mishael and Elzaphan would later carry the bodies of Nadab and Abihu out of the camp (Leviticus 10:4).

23.brief: Aaron marries Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, and she bears Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. The line of Aaron’s sons, who will serve as priests, is recorded.
23.explain:
“Aaron took to himself Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon, as wife;”

Aaron married Elisheba. She came from the tribe of Judah. Her brother Nahshon became the leader of Judah (Numbers 2:3) and appears in the line of David (Ruth 4:20).

“and she bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.”

Aaron’s four sons would become priests. Nadab and Abihu died for offering strange fire (Leviticus 10:1–2). Eleazar succeeded Aaron as high priest (Numbers 20:28). The line of Aaron’s sons, who will serve as priests, is recorded.
23.notes: The name Elisheba is the Hebrew form of the name Elizabeth. Luke notes that Elizabeth, the mother of John the Baptist, was “of the daughters of Aaron” (Luke 1:5).

24.brief: The sons of Korah are Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph, the families of the Korahites. The record notes Korah’s descendants as part of Levi’s households.
24.explain:
“And the sons of Korah were Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These are the families of the Korahites.”

Korah’s descendants are named. Though Korah later rebelled, his sons did not die with him (Numbers 26:11). Their descendants later served as singers in the temple, and several psalms carry titles naming the sons of Korah (for example, Psalm 42).

25.brief: Aaron’s son Eleazar marries a daughter of Putiel, and she bears Phinehas. The genealogy ends with the heads of the Levite families, reaching to Aaron’s grandson.
25.explain:
“Eleazar, Aaron’s son, took for himself one of the daughters of Putiel as wife;”

Eleazar married a daughter of Putiel. Nothing else is known about Putiel.

“and she bore him Phinehas.”

Their son was Phinehas. He would later act zealously for the LORD and receive a covenant of perpetual priesthood (Numbers 25:7–13).

“These are the heads of the fathers’ houses of the Levites according to their families.”

The genealogy ends with the heads of the Levite families, reaching to Aaron’s grandson.

26.brief: The record closes by naming the same Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said, “Bring out the children of Israel from the land of Egypt according to their armies.” The genealogy’s purpose is stated: it identifies the very men God commissioned.
26.explain:
“These are the same Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said,”

The genealogy now states its purpose. It identifies “the same Aaron and Moses” God commissioned.

“Bring out the children of Israel from the land of Egypt according to their armies.”

God’s command repeats the mission. Israel will leave “according to their armies,” in organized ranks, like troops. The slaves will march out as the LORD’s army. The genealogy’s purpose is stated: it identifies the very men God commissioned.
26.notes: The phrase “according to their armies” appears again in 12:51, and Israel is called the LORD’s armies in 7:4 and 12:41. It pictures Israel leaving Egypt in orderly divisions.

27.brief: Aaron and Moses are the ones who spoke to Pharaoh to bring Israel out of Egypt, “the same Moses and Aaron.” The repeated identification returns the reader to the story of their mission.
27.explain:
“These are the ones who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring out the children of Israel from Egypt.”

The record names the two brothers again as the ones who confronted Pharaoh.

“These are the same Moses and Aaron.”

The repeated identification returns the reader to the story of their mission. In 6:26 Aaron is named first, as the older brother. Here Moses is named first, as the leader.

28.brief: The narrative resumes on the day the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt. The account picks up where it paused in verse 12.
28.explain:
“And it came to pass, on the day the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,”

The narrative resumes where it paused. The account picks up where it paused in 6:12, on the day God spoke to Moses in Egypt.

29.brief: The LORD says to Moses, “I am the LORD,” and commands him to speak to Pharaoh all that He says. Moses’ task rests again on God’s name and God’s words.
29.explain:
“that the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, ‘I am the LORD.”

God speaks His name again. Moses’ task rests on who God is.

“Speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt all that I say to you.”

Moses must speak “all that I say to you.” He must deliver God’s message without adding or subtracting. Moses’ task rests again on God’s name and God’s words.

30.brief: Moses again protests that he is of uncircumcised lips and asks how Pharaoh will heed him. His repeated objection frames the genealogy and prepares for God’s answer in Exodus 7:1.
30.explain:
“But Moses said before the LORD, ‘Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips, and how shall Pharaoh heed me?”

Moses repeats his objection from 6:12. He still feels unfit to speak. His repeated objection frames the genealogy and prepares for God’s answer in 7:1. God does not dismiss Moses’ weakness. He answers it by assigning Aaron to speak and by promising His own power.
